records.name: William Byrd I
records.scaleNote: Encyclopedia Virginia says Byrd 'underwrote the importation of servants and slaves' for his own fields and for resale, and that importing Africans earned a share of the headrights behind his almost 30,000 acres; no voyage count survives.
records.origins: Born in London around 1652 to a goldsmith, Byrd came to Virginia to inherit an uncle's land and Indian-trade business at the falls of the James. He moved from Nathaniel Bacon's circle to Governor Berkeley's side after 1676 and rose to the Council (1683–1704) and the posts of auditor- and receiver-general.
records.role_summary: An Indian trader and merchant, Byrd imported indentured servants and enslaved Africans both to work his own tobacco land and to sell to other planters. Each person imported earned him a 50-acre headright, so the trade in people built the land base he passed to his son. He bought Westover in 1688 and died there in 1704.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia records that he underwrote imports of servants and slaves for his own use and for resale to other planters.
More than half his almost 30,000 acres came through headrights, and about a third of those headrights came from importing Africans (per Encyclopedia Virginia).
He bought the c. 1,000-acre Westover tract in 1688; it stayed with the Byrds until 1814.

records.legacy: His son William Byrd II inherited Westover and the land, built the brick mansion and laid out Richmond. The family fortune collapsed under William Byrd III, but the Byrd name stayed politically powerful in Virginia into the 20th century.

legacyDetail.d: Later Byrds included the Westover diarist William Byrd II and, among later descendants, Governor and Senator Harry F. Byrd Sr.

lineage.name: Mary Horsmanden Filmer
lineage.note: Married c. 1673; widow of Samuel Filmer and daughter of Warham Horsmanden.

lineage.name: William Byrd II
lineage.note: Inherited Westover and the land and enslaved people.

lineage.name: Ursula Byrd Beverley
lineage.note: Married the historian Robert Beverley, linking the Byrds to the Beverley family.

records.today: Westover passed out of the family in 1814 and has been owned by the Crane, Fisher and Erda families since 1921; the owners say they are researching the enslaved people who lived there. For later Byrd descendants see the Byrd family record.

records.name: Byrd family of Westover (William Byrd II & III)
records.scaleNote: William Byrd III took over an estate of more than 179,000 acres and 'hundreds of slaves' (Encyclopedia Virginia); exact counts do not survive.
records.origins: William Byrd II (1674–1744), educated in England, inherited his father's land, Westover and the enslaved people there in 1704. He sat on the Council for decades and is known for his secret diaries and his Dividing Line survey.
records.role_summary: Byrd II rebuilt Westover in brick (completed c. 1735) with enslaved labour and in 1733 planned Richmond and Petersburg; Richmond was laid out on his land and sold as lots from 1737. His son William Byrd III ran up huge debts: by 1767 trustees had sold land and enslaved people worth £40,000, and in 1768 he held a lottery of estate property valued at £56,796. In 1781 the British under Benedict Arnold carried off 49 enslaved people from Westover.

roleDetail.d: Historic Westover says the number enslaved under Byrd II is unknown but 'probably numbered in the hundreds'; NPS notes he sometimes sold enslaved people to pay debts.
Byrd II announced the surveyed town of Richmond in the Virginia Gazette on 22 April 1737; the city later became the Upper South's largest slave market.

roleDetail.t: Debt and sales under Byrd III.
roleDetail.d: Trustees sold land and enslaved people worth £40,000 by 1767; Byrd III mortgaged enslaved people and died by suicide at Westover in January 1777.
His widow sold other property to keep Westover and tried under a flag of truce to recover 49 enslaved people, horses and ferryboats seized by Arnold's force in 1781.

records.legacy: Westover left the family on Mary Willing Byrd's death in 1814. Later descendants included the Byrd brothers of Winchester — Governor and Senator Harry F. Byrd Sr., architect of 'Massive Resistance' to school desegregation, and polar explorer Richard E. Byrd. Virginia removed Harry Byrd's statue from Capitol Square on 7 July 2021.

legacyDetail.d: Harry F. Byrd Sr. (1887–1966), whose ancestors included William Byrd II, led Virginia's resistance to integration after 1954; the General Assembly voted in 2021 to remove his statue.

records.name: Robert "King" Carter
records.scaleNote: He held at least 295,000 acres at his death (Encyclopedia Virginia); estimates of the people he enslaved range from c. 700 to well over 1,000, so the figure is estimated.
records.origins: Son of the immigrant John Carter of Corotoman on the Rappahannock, he inherited land and enslaved people and became a burgess, Council member and acting governor (1726–27). He was agent for the Fairfax proprietors of the Northern Neck in 1702–11 and 1722–32.
records.role_summary: Carter was the richest planter of his generation. He acted as an agent for slave traders, bought captives from ships for his many quarters, and used his Northern Neck agency to steer vast land grants to himself and his children. He built the colony's largest house at Corotoman (burned 1729) and began Christ Church, Lancaster.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia notes he acted as an agent selling enslaved Africans from arriving ships, as well as buying them for his own quarters.
As Northern Neck agent he had surveyors locate land he could patent for his family; he died with at least 295,000 acres.
His children married into the Burwell, Page, Harrison, Fitzhugh and other families, spreading Carter land and enslaved people across Tidewater Virginia.

records.legacy: His estate seeded many of Virginia's great houses: Carter's Grove, Shirley (through his son John), Sabine Hall (Landon Carter) and Nomini Hall (grandson Robert Carter III). Christ Church, Lancaster (completed c. 1735) is now a museum that researches the Carter papers and the people enslaved at Corotoman.

legacyDetail.d: The Foundation for Historic Christ Church publishes his letters and diary and research on the enslaved people of Corotoman and on Robert Carter III's Deed of Gift.

records.name: Robert Carter III
records.scaleNote: His 1791 Deed of Gift set out the gradual freedom of more than 500 people (Encyclopedia Virginia; the Nomini Hall Slave Legacy project counts 511, Christ Church research 452) — probably the largest individual emancipation in the U.S. before 1860.
records.origins: Grandson of Robert 'King' Carter, he inherited Nomini Hall and a fortune in land and enslaved people, and sat on the colonial Council. He converted to evangelical Christianity in 1777, became a Baptist in 1778 and a Swedenborgian in 1788.
records.role_summary: For decades Carter enslaved hundreds of people on some 18 plantations in several counties. On 1 August 1791 he executed a Deed of Gift under Virginia's 1782 manumission law, freeing people in stages by age; executors were still carrying it out decades later. He moved to Baltimore in 1793 and died there in 1804.

roleDetail.d: Filed in Northumberland County, it freed adults on a schedule and children as they came of age, to limit resistance from neighbours and the law.
Encyclopedia Virginia says more than 500; Christ Church research counts 452; the Nomini Hall Slave Legacy project 511 across 18 plantations.
His Baptist and Swedenborgian convictions are usually given as the reason for the emancipation.

records.legacy: The Deed of Gift is the best-known counter-example among Virginia's great planters, who otherwise almost never freed people in large numbers. The Nomini Hall Slave Legacy project traces the freed people and their descendants.

legacyDetail.d: The Nomini Hall Slave Legacy project publishes a timeline, names and family histories of the people freed.

records.name: Carter family (Corotoman, Shirley, Sabine Hall)
records.scaleNote: At Shirley alone the 1787 tax list records Charles Hill Carter with 67 enslaved people over 16 and 67 younger (per Wikipedia's summary of the census); 70–90 people were enslaved there each year in the 19th century.
records.base: Shirley Plantation, Charles City County, Virginia
records.origins: Descended from the immigrant John Carter and his son Robert 'King' Carter. King Carter's son John married Elizabeth Hill, heiress of Shirley on the James, in the 1720s, founding the Hill Carter line; another son, Landon Carter, built Sabine Hall and kept a famous diary of plantation management.
records.role_summary: Across several branches the Carters were among Virginia's largest enslavers for two centuries. At Shirley, enslaved people farmed, cooked, cleaned and built; Landon Carter's diary records the daily coercion and resistance of the people at Sabine Hall. After 1865 Hill Carter had to divide the estate once unpaid labour ended.

roleDetail.d: Charles Hill Carter was taxed for 134 enslaved people at Shirley in 1787; 70–90 were held there yearly in the 19th century.
Encyclopedia Virginia describes Landon Carter (1710–1778) of Sabine Hall, whose diary is a key record of slavery and resistance on a Virginia estate.

records.legacy: Shirley, settled in 1613–14 and held by the Hill and Carter family since the 1600s, is often described as the oldest family-owned business in North America. It is still a working farm and house museum run by the 11th generation.

legacyDetail.d: The current owners describe themselves as the 11th generation on the land and their children as the 12th.

records.name: Randolph family of Virginia (Turkey Island, Tuckahoe)
records.scaleNote: William Randolph claimed headrights for 168 enslaved people and servants he brought in; his sons held about eleven large plantations worked by hundreds of enslaved people (per Wikipedia summarising Cowden's prosopography); totals are estimated.
records.origins: William Randolph (c. 1650–1711) came from Warwickshire, built a fortune in land, tobacco and trade at Turkey Island on the James, and married Mary Isham; they are often called the 'Adam and Eve of Virginia'. Their sons founded Tuckahoe, Dungeness, Curles, Chatsworth and other estates.
records.role_summary: The Randolphs were the most interconnected political family of colonial Virginia — Peyton Randolph, Edmund Randolph, Jefferson (through his mother Jane Randolph) and John Marshall were descendants or kin — and their wealth rested on enslaved labour. Family wills and inventories (for example Peyton Randolph's 1776 inventory of 27 enslaved people, including Eve) show people passed as property among the branches.

roleDetail.d: William Randolph claimed land for bringing 168 enslaved people and indentured servants into Virginia.
Ryland Randolph of Turkey Island willed Aggy her freedom in 1784, but administrators kept her enslaved; a Henrico court ordered her and her two children freed in 1790.
Thomas Mann Randolph married Martha Jefferson; their son Thomas Jefferson Randolph ran the 1827 Monticello sale and in 1832 proposed gradual emancipation in the legislature.

records.legacy: Turkey Island's mansion burned in 1806; Tuckahoe survives as a private house museum. Randolph descendants include both Jefferson's white family and, through the Hemings family, Black descendants recognised by Monticello's Getting Word project.

legacyDetail.d: The Randolph line carries Jefferson's white descendants (Monticello Association); see thomas-jefferson for the Hemings–Randolph reckoning.

records.name: John Randolph of Roanoke
records.scaleNote: His contested wills led to the 1846 freeing of about 383 people (sources give 383 to nearly 400), who were resettled in Ohio.
records.origins: A Randolph of the Curles/Bizarre branch and stepson of St. George Tucker, he inherited land and enslaved people and became a sharp-tongued states'-rights congressman (various terms 1799–1833), senator (1825–27) and minister to Russia (1830).
records.role_summary: Randolph defended slavery as a political matter while holding hundreds of people at Roanoke. He wrote wills in 1819, 1821 and 1832; the first two freed his enslaved people and funded land for them outside Virginia, the third did not, and he repudiated it on his deathbed. After years of litigation by relatives, a court upheld the 1821 will and the people were freed in 1846.

roleDetail.d: Relatives contested the wills on grounds of insanity; freedom came only in 1846, 13 years after his death.
Executor William Leigh bought about 3,200 acres in Mercer County, Ohio, but armed white residents turned the 383 freedpeople away in 1846; many settled at Rossville near Piqua and in Shelby County.

records.legacy: Descendants of the Randolph Freedpeople remain in western Ohio and have campaigned to tell the story and seek justice for the land they were denied. Randolph-Macon College was named in part for him.

legacyDetail.d: Ohio historians and descendants have marked Rossville and pressed for recognition of the lost Mercer County land (WYSU, 2024).
Gregory May's 'A Madman's Will' (2023) retells the will fight and the Ohio resettlement.

records.name: Harrison family of Berkeley
records.scaleNote: Berkeley credits Benjamin Harrison V with 110 enslaved people, listed by family in his 1791 estate inventory.
records.base: Berkeley Plantation, Charles City County, Virginia
records.origins: Benjamin Harrison III bought Berkeley on the James in 1691 and ran the river's first successful shipyard. Benjamin Harrison IV, who married King Carter's daughter Anne, built the brick mansion in 1726.
records.role_summary: Enslaved people grew tobacco and worked in the house and shipyard at Berkeley, sometimes up to 16 hours a day at harvest. Benjamin Harrison V (1726–1791) signed the Declaration of Independence and was governor (1781–84); his son William Henry Harrison was born there in 1773 and became the ninth president, and his great-grandson Benjamin Harrison the 23rd.

roleDetail.d: Benjamin Harrison V's estate inventory lists the 110 people he enslaved in genealogical order — elder first, then descendants — unusual for the period; a copy is shown at Berkeley.
William Henry Harrison grew up on the slave-worked estate; as Indiana territorial governor (1800–12) he presided over indenture laws that allowed de facto slavery.

records.legacy: The Harrisons held Berkeley for more than 150 years until Benjamin Harrison VIII. The Jamieson family has owned it since the early 20th century and says it is working with researchers on the history of the enslaved; reconstructed quarters from the film 'Harriet' (built 2018) now stand near the original quarter site.

legacyDetail.d: Berkeley's 'Berkeley's Enslaved' page describes field and house labour and invites descendants and researchers to share information.

records.name: Page family of Rosewell
records.scaleNote: Rosewell was built and run by enslaved workers; most 18th-century Gloucester records burned, so totals are estimated (local studies document at least 111 people in the 18th century).
records.origins: Mann Page I (c. 1691–1730), grandson of the immigrant John Page, married Judith Carter, daughter of Robert 'King' Carter, and began Rosewell on the York River in 1725 — one of the largest houses in colonial America.
records.role_summary: NPS describes Rosewell as built with wealth from enslaved labour, agriculture and Atlantic trade; a marker records that it was built by European craftsmen, indentured servants and enslaved Africans. The Pages married into nearly every great Tidewater family, and Governor John Page (1743–1808), Jefferson's friend, grew up there.

roleDetail.d: The NPS Chesapeake gateways listing for the Rosewell ruin says enslaved and free African Americans built and maintained the plantation.
Rosewell's cost left heavy debts; the family sold part of the estate in 1793 and the house left Page hands in the 1830s.

records.legacy: Rosewell burned in 1916 and survives as a ruin managed with archaeology programmes. The Page–Nelson descendant Thomas Nelson Page (1853–1922) became the leading 'plantation school' novelist, romanticising slavery in fiction such as 'In Ole Virginia' (1887).

legacyDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia describes Thomas Nelson Page's nostalgic dialect stories of loyal enslaved people, which shaped national memory of the plantation South.

records.name: Nelson family of Yorktown
records.scaleNote: About 8,500 enslaved Africans were imported into the York River in 1718–27 while 'Scotch Tom' Nelson sold captives on consignment there (Christ's College Cambridge); his personal share is unknown. Thomas Nelson Jr. sold 120 people in 1788.
records.origins: Thomas 'Scotch Tom' Nelson (1677–1745), from Cumberland, settled at Yorktown in the early 1700s as a merchant, ferry and mill owner. The family store, wharf and ship 'Nelson' made them the leading York River merchants.
records.role_summary: Scotch Tom sold enslaved Africans on consignment for English firms and shipped corn and pork to Barbados; his son William Nelson (1711–1772), President of the Council, imported enslaved people into Virginia and occasionally Maryland and Pennsylvania. Grandson Thomas Nelson Jr. (1738–1789), a signer and governor in 1781, bought 5,400 acres and enslaved people from Lewis Burwell and was forced by debt to sell 120 people in Prince William County in 1788.

roleDetail.d: Christ's College's legacies research says Scotch Tom sold enslaved people for English firms during the York River import boom.
Thomas Nelson Jr.'s will left named people, including Aggy, her son Charles and Melinda, to his children.

records.legacy: The Nelson House in Yorktown, built c. 1730, was acquired by the National Park Service in 1968. Thomas Nelson Jr. studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, which now lists him in its 'Legacies of Enslavement' research.

legacyDetail.d: Christ's College, Cambridge documents the Nelsons' slave trading as part of its review of enslavement links.

records.name: Fitzhugh family (Bedford, Ravensworth, Chatham)
records.scaleNote: William Fitzhugh of Chatham kept quarters for 50 and in 1797 advertised about 230 enslaved people for sale with the estate (NPS).
records.origins: William Fitzhugh (1651–1701), an English lawyer, built a 54,000-acre estate in the Northern Neck, including Ravensworth in Fairfax County. His letters of 1679–1699 are a classic record of a planter building wealth from tobacco and bound labour.
records.role_summary: Fitzhugh's letters show him buying enslaved people and directing his quarters; his 1686 letter offering Bedford for sale lists 29 enslaved people, most 'country born'. His great-grandson William Fitzhugh (1741–1809) had Chatham built by enslaved craftsmen (completed c. 1771); after a 1805 revolt at Chatham, Abraham was executed and Robin and Cupid were sold away.

roleDetail.d: When overseer Starke cut the Christmas holiday short, the enslaved community bound and whipped him; Philip was killed in the suppression, James drowned fleeing, Abraham was hanged and Robin and Cupid transported.
Fitzhugh advertised about 230 enslaved people with Chatham in 1797; it took nine years to sell and families were sold off gradually.
The 1686 letter's count of 29 enslaved people is widely quoted from the published Fitzhugh letters; it is cited here from that tradition.

records.legacy: Chatham's daughter Mary Lee Fitzhugh married George Washington Parke Custis; their daughter Mary Anna Custis married Robert E. Lee, so Fitzhugh, Custis and Lee estates and enslaved people were joined at Arlington. Chatham is now part of Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park.

legacyDetail.d: Lee's son William Henry Fitzhugh 'Rooney' Lee carried the family name; Ravensworth passed through Fitzhugh heirs to the Lees.

records.name: George Mason IV
records.scaleNote: Gunston Hall says Mason enslaved at least 300 people over his life; he inherited 35 and freed none.
records.origins: Heir to a Potomac planting family, Mason inherited land and 35 enslaved people from his father. Gunston Hall was built by enslaved and paid workers in 1755–59.
records.role_summary: Mason drafted the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776) and at the 1787 Convention condemned the foreign slave trade (22 August) and refused to sign the Constitution, partly over its protection of the trade until 1808. Yet he enslaved at least 300 people, listed 36 by name in his 1773 will as property for his children, and freed no one.

roleDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia notes he condemned slavery but saw ending imports as disturbing few vested interests — Virginia had a surplus of enslaved people to sell.
Named 36 enslaved people to pass, with their 'increase', to his children at 21 or marriage.

records.legacy: George Mason University (named 1957/1972) dedicated the Enslaved People of George Mason Memorial on 4 April 2022, after student research begun in 2017. Gunston Hall, owned by the Commonwealth, interprets the enslaved community and Mason's contradictions.

legacyDetail.d: The Wilkins Plaza memorial names people Mason enslaved, including children, and sits beside his statue.

records.name: Tayloe family of Mount Airy
records.scaleNote: Colonial Williamsburg records that 875 people were enslaved by the Tayloes on Mount Airy between 1808 and 1865; skilled enslaved workers also ran their Neabsco and Occoquan ironworks.
records.origins: John Tayloe I (1687–1747) built a fortune in land and the Neabsco iron furnace; John Tayloe II (1721–1779) built Mount Airy (c. 1748–58) on the Rappahannock. John Tayloe III (1771–1828) was said to be the richest Virginian of his day and built the Octagon House in Washington.
records.role_summary: Enslaved founders, fillers, miners, colliers and ship carpenters made the Tayloe ironworks profitable until iron production ended around 1800; at Mount Airy they grew tobacco and wheat and kept hogs. The family moved people to Alabama cotton plantations — Winney Grimshaw, born at Mount Airy in 1826, was sent to Alabama as punishment after her father escaped to Canada.

roleDetail.d: Laura Croghan Kamoie's 'Irons in the Fire' (2007) shows enslaved labour underpinned the Tayloe iron business.
Tayloe heirs shifted enslaved people from Virginia to Alabama plantations in the 1830s–50s.

records.legacy: Mount Airy remains in Tayloe hands — the 10th generation now runs it as a farm and event estate. The family's records underpin Richard Dunn's comparative study 'A Tale of Two Plantations' (2014), which follows Mount Airy's enslaved families.

legacyDetail.d: Tayloe III's Washington townhouse (built 1799–1801) is now a museum of the American Architectural Foundation; enslaved Tayloe workers lived and laboured there.

records.name: Wormeley family of Rosegill
records.scaleNote: Few numbers survive; after Bacon's Rebellion Ralph Wormeley II bought enslaved people imported from the Caribbean, and more than 30 were carried off in a 1781 British raid on Rosegill.
records.origins: Ralph Wormeley I moved the family seat to Rosegill on the Rappahannock before his death in 1651. Ralph Wormeley II (1651–1701), Oxford-educated, became secretary of the colony and a Council member.
records.role_summary: Ralph Wormeley II expanded Rosegill and ran several Tidewater plantations with enslaved labour, buying people shipped from the Caribbean in the switch from indentured to enslaved labour after 1676. Later Wormeleys were Loyalists in the Revolution and lost enslaved people to a 1781 British raid.

roleDetail.d: Wormeley's purchases of Caribbean-shipped Africans illustrate how the Tidewater elite shifted to enslaved labour in the 1680s–90s.
British raiders looted Rosegill; more than 30 enslaved people were recovered sick with smallpox.

records.legacy: Rosegill survives as a private house on the National Register. The Wormeley line faded after the Revolution; the family is an example of early Council-class wealth built on bound labour.

legacyDetail.d: Ralph Wormeley V's loyalism cost the family political standing after 1776.

records.name: Burwell family (Fairfield, Carter's Grove)
records.scaleNote: Carter Burwell held more than 90 enslaved people and 3,000+ acres when Carter's Grove was finished (Encyclopedia Virginia); Lewis Burwell later sold Thomas Nelson Jr. 5,400 acres with enslaved people.
records.base: Carter's Grove, James City County, Virginia
records.origins: The Burwells of Fairfield, Gloucester County, were Council-class planters from the 1600s. Nathaniel Burwell married Elizabeth Carter, daughter of King Carter; their son Carter Burwell (1716–1756) inherited a 1,400-acre tract under King Carter's will.
records.role_summary: Carter Burwell built the brick mansion at Carter's Grove (1751–55) with enslaved labour and held more than 90 people. The family's enslaved workforce supported Fairfield, Carter's Grove and later Shenandoah estates.

roleDetail.d: Named for King Carter, the house is one of Virginia's finest Georgian mansions and was built by enslaved and hired workers.
Lewis Burwell sold Thomas Nelson Jr. 5,400 acres and enslaved people during the Revolution.

records.legacy: Carter's Grove later passed to the Rockefeller-funded Colonial Williamsburg Foundation, which reconstructed slave quarters there; it was sold in 2007 to Halsey Minor for $15.3 million, fell into bankruptcy, and was sold in 2014 to Samuel Mencoff for $7.5 million.

legacyDetail.d: Colonial Williamsburg's reconstructed slave quarter at Carter's Grove closed with the sale; the property is now private.

records.name: Bolling family (Kippax, Cobbs; 'Red Bollings')
records.scaleNote: Robert Bolling acquired land through headrights for importing servants and enslaved people (a 1690 grant names 'Tony a negro'); later Bollings were mid-sized Southside and Bedford County enslavers. Totals are not documented here.
records.base: Kippax Plantation, Prince George County, Virginia
records.origins: Robert Bolling (1646–1709), a London-born merchant and part ship-owner, married Jane Rolfe, granddaughter of Pocahontas, in 1674. Their only son John Bolling of Cobbs carried the Pocahontas line; descendants of Robert's second marriage are informally called 'White Bollings'.
records.role_summary: The Bollings were Appomattox River merchants and planters whose land came partly from headrights on imported people. Descent from Pocahontas through the Bollings became a mark of status among Virginia elites — prized even as the same families enslaved Africans and passed racial-integrity laws.

roleDetail.d: Robert Bolling's 1690 land grant lists 'Tony a negro' among the people he transported.
Virginia's 1924 Racial Integrity Act included a 'Pocahontas exception' to protect elite descendants like the Bollings and Randolphs.

records.legacy: Edith Bolling Galt Wilson (1872–1961), second wife of Woodrow Wilson, was a 'Red Bolling'; her family had enslaved people on its Bedford County plantation before the Civil War, and some formerly enslaved workers moved with them to Wytheville. Her birthplace in Wytheville is a museum.

legacyDetail.d: Encyclopedia Virginia notes Edith Bolling Wilson's pride in her Pocahontas descent.

records.name: John Hartwell Cocke (Bremo)
records.scaleNote: Taxed for 89 enslaved people aged 12+ in 1816 and 107 in 1830; reported 135 in Virginia and Alabama in 1860 (Encyclopedia Virginia).
records.origins: From the Cocke planter family of Surry County, he inherited the 3,100-acre Bremo plantation and moved there in 1809. He helped Jefferson found the University of Virginia and sat on its board (1819–56).
records.role_summary: Cocke called slavery a curse and was vice president of the American Colonization Society (1819–66), but freed only those he judged 'qualified' for Liberia. He sent the stonemason Peyton Skipwith and his family to Liberia in 1833, bought an Alabama cotton plantation in the early 1840s as a 'school' for freedom, and by 1860 had approved only 14 people.

roleDetail.d: His 1841 terms required people to earn their value, renounce alcohol and keep the plan secret before being freed for Liberia.
Enslaved people including Skipwith quarried stone for UVA buildings under Cocke's oversight.

records.legacy: The letters the Skipwith family sent him from Liberia (1834–65), held at UVA's Small Special Collections Library, are among the fullest records left by a formerly enslaved family. UVA's Cocke Hall bears his name.

legacyDetail.d: Published as 'Dear Master: Letters of a Slave Family' (ed. Randall M. Miller, 1978).

lineage.name: Louisa Maxwell Holmes Cocke
lineage.note: Second wife; also active in colonization.

lineage.name: Peyton Skipwith

records.today: No publicly documented descendants speak for the Cocke family. Bremo remains a private estate and National Historic Landmark.

records.name: Peyton Skipwith
records.scaleNote: Known through more than 200 letters (1834–65) by him and his children, held at UVA and published as 'Dear Master' (1978).
records.base: Bremo, Fluvanna County, Virginia → Monrovia, Liberia
records.origins: Born enslaved on John Hartwell Cocke's Bremo estate, Skipwith became a skilled stonemason who quarried and cut stone for University of Virginia buildings.
records.role_summary: Cocke freed Skipwith and his family in 1833 on condition they emigrate to Liberia under the American Colonization Society. His wife and a daughter died within the first year; Skipwith wrote frankly to Cocke about disease, hunger, conflict with local peoples and the colony's politics.

roleDetail.d: Like many manumissions of the era, freedom required leaving the United States.
His daughter Diana Skipwith and other relatives continued the correspondence to 1865.

records.legacy: The Skipwith letters are a core source on Americo-Liberian settlement.

legacyDetail.d: Randall M. Miller's edition 'Dear Master' (UGA Press) keeps the letters in print.

records.name: Lee family of Stratford Hall
records.scaleNote: About 200 enslaved people lived at Stratford and other Thomas Lee properties by c. 1742 (Stratford Hall); Philip Ludwell Lee left 137 to his heirs in 1775 (Encyclopedia Virginia).
records.origins: Thomas Lee (1690–1750), acting governor and founder of the Ohio Company, bought the Stratford land in 1717 and built the Great House c. 1738–early 1740s. In 1738 the ship Liverpool Merchant brought 70 enslaved Africans to the Potomac for sale; some may have been bought to build it.
records.role_summary: Enslaved people made bricks, built and ran Stratford, worked its fields and served in the house. Thomas Lee's sons Richard Henry Lee and Francis Lightfoot Lee signed the Declaration; in 1769 Richard Henry helped launch a boycott that included 'slaves from Africa and the West Indies' while the family kept enslaving people at home.

roleDetail.d: He bequeathed 137 enslaved workers in 1775; the 1860 census still counted 31 at Stratford.
Henry Lee IV sold Stratford in 1822 after embezzling from his ward; it was later auctioned.

records.legacy: The Robert E. Lee Memorial Association bought Stratford in 1929 for $240,000 and runs it as a museum that now researches and names the enslaved community; in 2023 it held public events honouring the people who built the Lees' wealth.

legacyDetail.d: WVTF reported in 2023 on Stratford's work to centre enslaved people in tours.

records.name: James Madison
records.scaleNote: Madison enslaved more than 100 people (Encyclopedia Virginia); Montpelier counts about 300 people enslaved there across the Madison years.
records.origins: Eldest son of a Piedmont planting family, Madison grew up at Montpelier, which his grandparents had settled with enslaved workers in the 1720s. He inherited the estate and its enslaved community.
records.role_summary: Madison defended the three-fifths clause in Federalist No. 54, served as fourth president (1809–17) with enslaved staff such as Paul Jennings in the White House, and became president of the American Colonization Society in 1833. He sold 16 enslaved people to a relative in Louisiana in 1834 to pay debts and freed no one; after his death Dolley Madison sold Montpelier in 1844 and split up the community.

roleDetail.d: Despite calling slavery an evil, he did not free the people he enslaved and doubted Black and white Americans could live together free.
Dolley transferred some 50 enslaved people to her son John Payne Todd, sold others with the estate and to dealers.

records.legacy: Montpelier, owned by the National Trust and run by the Montpelier Foundation, opened 'The Mere Distinction of Colour' exhibit (2017) and in 2021–22 committed to 'structural parity' with descendants of the enslaved on its board — a first among presidential sites.

legacyDetail.d: After a March 2022 reversal drew criticism from the National Trust, the board elected 11 members nominated by the Montpelier Descendants Committee.

records.name: Paul Jennings
records.scaleNote: Author of 'A Colored Man's Reminiscences of James Madison' (1863/1865), considered the first White House memoir; well documented by Montpelier and the White House Historical Association.
records.origins: Born enslaved at Montpelier in 1799, Jennings was taken to the President's House as a footman in 1809, aged ten.
records.role_summary: He was present when the White House was evacuated on 24 August 1814 and said he and others saved Gilbert Stuart's Washington portrait. As Madison's valet from about 1820 he witnessed Madison's death in 1836. Dolley Madison's 1841 will promised freedom, but she sold him in 1846; Senator Daniel Webster bought his freedom in 1847, and he likely helped plan the 1848 'Pearl' escape attempt.

roleDetail.d: Sold to Pollard Webb for $200 in 1846; Webster paid $120 and Jennings worked off the rest.
77 enslaved people tried to flee Washington on the schooner Pearl on 15 April 1848; authorities never learned of Jennings's role.

records.legacy: His sons John, Franklin and William served in the Union army. His descendants held a reunion at Montpelier and toured the White House on 24 August 2009, the 195th anniversary of the portrait's rescue.

legacyDetail.d: NPR reported a dozen or more descendants posing before the portrait Jennings helped save.

Descendant A. Raleigh Marshall, who learned of the link in 2008, speaks publicly about it and sits on an advisory board at James Madison University.

records.name: James Monroe
records.scaleNote: Documents show Monroe enslaved at least 178 people over his life; the 1810 census counted 49 adults at Highland; in 1828 he sold 17 to Florida (Encyclopedia Virginia).
records.origins: Son of a modest Westmoreland County planter, Monroe built Highland next to Jefferson's Monticello in the 1790s. As governor in 1800 he oversaw the suppression and executions after Gabriel's planned revolt.
records.role_summary: Monroe was fifth president (1817–25) and a backer of the American Colonization Society; Liberia's capital, Monrovia, was named for him. Chronically in debt, he sold 17 members of Highland's enslaved community to Colonel Joseph White's Casa Bianca cotton plantation in Jefferson County, Florida, in 1828, and others locally.

roleDetail.d: As governor he directed the response to the 1800 plot; about 26 men, including Gabriel, were hanged.
The 17 people sold in 1828 stayed together as families at Casa Bianca beyond the Civil War.

records.legacy: William & Mary has owned Highland since 1974; since 2017 it has worked with descendants and in 2019 formed a Council of Descendant Advisors. Descendants of people Monroe sold or enslaved live in Monroetown near Highland and in Florida.

legacyDetail.d: Highland's advisors shape exhibits and research, including the 'Take Them In Families' project on the 1828 sale.

records.name: John Tyler
records.scaleNote: Census counts: 24 enslaved at Greenway (1820), 46 at Sherwood Forest (1850), 43 (1860); Julia Tyler described 60–70 in 1844 (Sherwood Forest).
records.base: Sherwood Forest, Charles City County, Virginia
records.origins: Son of Governor John Tyler Sr. of Greenway, Charles City County, he inherited enslaved people and became governor, senator, vice president and, on William Henry Harrison's death in 1841, tenth president.
records.role_summary: A lifelong enslaver who called slavery a 'necessary evil', Tyler argued that spreading slavery west would 'diffuse' it; he signed the 1845 annexation of Texas as a slave state. He sold people including Ned (1857, $1,200), voted for secession and was elected to the Confederate Congress before dying in January 1862, having freed no one.

roleDetail.d: Secretary of State Calhoun openly linked annexation to slavery; Tyler signed the joint resolution in March 1845.
Sherwood Forest's own research names more than 40 people, including the Short, Black and Hall families; Roscius Short escaped and joined the 1st U.S. Colored Cavalry.

records.legacy: Sherwood Forest has stayed in the Tyler family; Harrison Ruffin Tyler (1928–2025), the president's grandson and co-founder of ChemTreat, bought it from cousins in 1975 and restored it. It is now held by a private Tyler family foundation that has published research on the people Tyler enslaved.

legacyDetail.d: In 2021 W&M renamed its history department from Lyon G. Tyler (the president's son, a Confederacy apologist) to Harrison Ruffin Tyler, its donor.

records.name: Patrick Henry
records.scaleNote: He held 67 enslaved people at Red Hill at his death in 1799, and about 45 more on other holdings (Red Hill; Jefferson School/PHS research).
records.origins: Son of a Hanover County planter, Henry received six enslaved people and the Pine Slash farm as his wife Sarah Shelton's dowry in 1754. He became Virginia's most famous orator and its first post-colonial governor.
records.role_summary: In 1773 Henry wrote, 'Would anyone believe I am the master of slaves of my own purchase... I will not, I cannot justify it' — yet kept buying and holding people. At Scotchtown his mentally ill wife was confined in a basement room cared for by an enslaved woman. His will let his widow choose 20 enslaved people and divided the other 47 among heirs.

roleDetail.d: His 1773 admission that slavery was wrong did not lead to any manumission.
Red Hill research traces how Dorothea Henry's household of enslaved people was later split up as she remarried and moved.

records.legacy: Red Hill (Patrick Henry National Memorial) and Scotchtown now research and name the people Henry enslaved, including the 'Fractured Community' programme on Dorothea Henry Winston's enslaved households.

legacyDetail.d: Henry and Patrick counties in Virginia, Patrick Henry College and many schools bear his name.

lineage.name: Sarah Shelton Henry

lineage.name: Dorothea Dandridge Henry

records.today: Henry has many descendants, mostly private; no public figure is documented speaking for the family. Red Hill and Scotchtown lead public reckoning.

records.name: George Wythe
records.scaleNote: A small enslaver who began freeing people after 1787 and owned none at his death (Encyclopedia Virginia).
records.origins: A Tidewater lawyer, Wythe was Jefferson's law teacher, a signer of the Declaration and America's first law professor (William & Mary, 1780–89).
records.role_summary: Wythe enslaved household workers, including some inherited from his wife, but after her death in 1787 freed Lydia Broadnax and later Benjamin (1797) and others, paying those who stayed. As chancellor he ruled in Hudgins v. Wrights (1806) that freedom was the presumption, a ruling overturned on appeal. He and the free youth Michael Brown, whom he was tutoring, were poisoned in 1806.

roleDetail.d: He freed Lydia Broadnax in 1787 and Benjamin in 1797; he owned no one at his death.
Broadnax survived the poisoning but Virginia law barred Black testimony against a white defendant, and his great-nephew Sweeney was acquitted of murder.

records.legacy: Wythe is remembered as an anti-slavery jurist; William & Mary's law school is named for him and the Wythe House is a Colonial Williamsburg landmark.

legacyDetail.d: Wythe County and Wytheville, Virginia, and William & Mary Law School's Wythe name.

records.name: Michael Brown (of the Wythe household)
records.scaleNote: Known from the 1806 poisoning case records and press reports collected by Encyclopedia Virginia.
records.origins: A free African American youth living in George Wythe's Richmond household, where Wythe tutored him in Latin and Greek.
records.role_summary: Brown, Wythe and Lydia Broadnax fell ill after breakfast on 25 May 1806; Brown died on 1 June and Wythe on 8 June. The indictment for Brown's murder was quashed without trial, and Sweeney was acquitted of Wythe's murder — a case widely blamed on the ban on Black testimony.

roleDetail.d: No one was tried for his death.

records.legacy: His story is told in Encyclopedia Virginia's primary-source collection on Wythe's death and in histories of Black education in early Richmond.

legacyDetail.d: Accounts of Wythe's death now name Brown and Broadnax as victims.

records.name: Robert Lumpkin
records.scaleNote: Only one partial ledger (1849–50, at the Valentine) survives, so the number of people held at his jail is unknown; it was among Richmond's best-known slave jails.
records.origins: A slave trader active in the Richmond trade, Lumpkin bought the Wall Street jail complex from the Bank of Virginia on 27 November 1844 for $6,000.
records.role_summary: Lumpkin bought and sold people himself and charged other traders and owners a daily fee to hold captives in his jail, with a boardinghouse for clients. Anthony Burns, returned from Boston under the Fugitive Slave Act, was held there about four months in 1854. Lumpkin had five or more children with Mary, a woman he enslaved, and sent them north for education.

roleDetail.d: The complex — called 'the Devil's Half Acre' — held people awaiting sale in Shockoe's auction rooms.
Burns's months in Lumpkin's jail left him crippled and ill.

records.legacy: After his death in 1866 Mary Lumpkin leased the jail to Rev. Nathaniel Colver, whose 1867 school there became Virginia Union University. The site was excavated in 2005–08 and is planned as the centre of Richmond's Shockoe memorial and National Slavery Museum.

legacyDetail.d: VUU traces its origins to classes held in the former jail.

lineage.name: Mary Lumpkin
lineage.note: Inherited the property in 1866.

lineage.name: Nathaniel Colver
lineage.note: Baptist minister who opened the Colver Institute in 1867.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants are identified here; the Lumpkin daughters married and lived in the North. The site is publicly owned and central to Richmond's memorial plans.

records.name: Mary Lumpkin
records.scaleNote: Documented in property and court records and in Kristen Green's history 'The Devil's Half Acre' (2022).
records.base: Richmond, Virginia; Philadelphia; New Richmond, Ohio
records.origins: Enslaved by the trader Robert Lumpkin from a young age, Mary was held in a coerced relationship with him; she bore several children while living at his jail compound.
records.role_summary: She secured education for her daughters, who attended a Massachusetts seminary in 1857–58, and moved with the children to Philadelphia during the Civil War to protect them from sale for Lumpkin's debts. Inheriting the jail in 1866, she leased it in May 1867 to Nathaniel Colver for a school for formerly enslaved men, the origin of Virginia Union University.

roleDetail.d: She sold the property in 1873 and later lived in Ohio.

records.legacy: She is now honoured as a founder figure of Virginia Union University and of Black higher education in Richmond.

legacyDetail.d: University lectures and Kristen Green's book have made her story widely known.

lineage.name: Robert Lumpkin
lineage.note: Left her the property.

lineage.name: Martha and Anna Lumpkin
lineage.note: Educated in Massachusetts.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants are named here.

records.name: Silas Omohundro
records.scaleNote: His records show at least 1,900 people jailed in 1851–61, with jail profits of $6,250.57 (Encyclopedia Virginia).
records.origins: A Virginia-born trader who built a jail, boardinghouse and home in Richmond's slave-trading district.
records.role_summary: Omohundro bought, held and sold people — for example a woman named Willy Ann for $1,400 in 1859 — and charged 30–40 cents a night to jail captives for other traders. He fathered seven children with Corinna Hinton, an enslaved girl who was 13 when the first was born in 1849; she clothed people for auction. His 1864 will freed her and the children.

roleDetail.d: His surviving accounts are one of the most detailed records of a Richmond jail business.

records.legacy: His estate (Richmond property appraised at $84,060, plus Pennsylvania homes) was settled for the children only in the 1880s.

legacyDetail.d: He is likely buried in an unmarked grave there.

lineage.name: Corinna Hinton
lineage.note: Freed by his will.

lineage.name: Silas Omohundro Jr.
lineage.note: First of their children.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants named.

records.name: Hector Davis
records.scaleNote: His auction house sold people with a market value of more than $2.67 million in 1859 alone (Encyclopedia Virginia).
records.origins: Born probably in Goochland County, Davis moved to Richmond in the 1840s and partnered with David M. Pulliam in the 1850s.
records.role_summary: Davis was one of Richmond's biggest auctioneers and ran a jail where people were held before sale; in early 1860 he and 13 others chartered the Traders Bank of Richmond, with him as president. He had four children with Ann Banks Davis, an enslaved woman; his 1859 will freed them and left $20,000 for their education.

roleDetail.d: The Traders Bank's notes were pitched to planters and merchants — finance and slave sales intertwined.
The 1865 fire and Confederate defeat wiped out the bequest; Ann and the children received nothing after lawsuits.

records.legacy: His son Audubon Davis became a journalist. The Davis auction site is part of the Richmond Slave Trail.

legacyDetail.d: Richmond's Slave Trail marks the Shockoe auction houses.

records.name: Bacon Tait
records.scaleNote: Shipped 37 people from Norfolk to New Orleans in 1828 and ran a Richmond jail from 1834; held about $130,000 in real estate by 1850 (Encyclopedia Virginia).
records.origins: Born near Lynchburg, Tait entered the interstate trade in the 1820s, partnering with Thomas Boudar, who sold in New Orleans.
records.role_summary: Tait sold Wall Street lots in 1833 on which Lewis Collier's jail — later Lumpkin's — was probably built (one scholar argues Tait built it), and in 1834 built his own jail at 15th and Cary. He served on Richmond City Council (1847–51) and in 1852 bought a house in Salem, Massachusetts, where he lived with Courtney Fountain, a free Black woman, and their four children, while keeping his Richmond business.

roleDetail.d: His 1828 Norfolk–New Orleans shipment shows the sea route of the domestic trade.

records.legacy: His wealth survived the war intact; he died in 1871 and is buried in Hollywood Cemetery.

legacyDetail.d: Like Lumpkin and Davis, he used the North to shelter a Black family while trading people in the South.

records.name: Lumpkin's Jail ('the Devil's Half Acre')
records.description: A slave jail complex on Wall Street (Lumpkin's Alley) in Shockoe Bottom, bought by Robert Lumpkin in 1844 for $6,000, where traders paid to hold people awaiting sale; Anthony Burns was held there in 1854. In 1867 Mary Lumpkin leased it for the Colver Institute, forerunner of Virginia Union University. Archaeologists found the jail nearly 15 feet below grade in 2005–08; it is one of 17 Richmond Slave Trail sites.

records.name: Shockoe Bottom slave market, Richmond
records.description: Richmond's auction houses and jails in Shockoe Bottom made the city the largest slave market of the Upper South and often called the second-busiest in the U.S. (1830–65); its sales ran to $7–8 million a year c. 1860 (Encyclopedia Virginia). Firms included Dickinson, Hill & Co., Pulliam & Co., Hector Davis, Silas Omohundro and Bacon Tait, who flew red flags on auction days. Richmond's 2024 master plan for a 10-acre Shockoe memorial district includes a planned National Slavery Museum.

sources.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — The Domestic Slave Trade in Virginia

records.name: Westover Plantation
records.description: James River plantation bought by William Byrd I in 1688; William Byrd II's brick mansion (c. 1735) was built and served by enslaved people probably numbering in the hundreds. The Byrds held it until 1814; private owners since 1921 display known names of the enslaved and are running archaeology with Virginia's Department of Historic Resources.

records.name: Berkeley Plantation
records.description: Charles City County estate of the Harrisons from 1691; the 1726 brick house was home to Benjamin Harrison V, who enslaved 110 people, and birthplace of William Henry Harrison. Now owned by the Jamieson family and open to visitors, with an exhibit on Berkeley's enslaved.

records.name: Gunston Hall
records.description: George Mason's Potomac plantation house, built 1755–59 by enslaved and paid workers on Mason Neck; Mason enslaved at least 300 people over his life. Now owned by the Commonwealth of Virginia and run as a museum that interprets the enslaved community.

sources.label: Gunston Hall — Enslaved People at Gunston Hall

records.name: Montpelier (James Madison's estate)
records.description: Orange County estate of the Madisons from the 1720s, where about 300 people were enslaved over the Madison years. Owned by the National Trust and run by the Montpelier Foundation, it pledged 'structural parity' with descendants of the enslaved in 2021 and, after a 2022 dispute, elected 11 board members nominated by the Montpelier Descendants Committee.

sources.label: History News Network — Montpelier board appoints 11 descendant nominees (2022)

records.name: Sherwood Forest Plantation
records.description: John Tyler's Charles City County plantation from the early 1840s, where 46 people were enslaved in 1850 and 43 in 1860. Still held by the Tyler family through a private foundation; Harrison Ruffin Tyler bought it from cousins in 1975 and restored it, and the site publishes research naming the people Tyler enslaved.

records.name: Robert Carter III's Deed of Gift (1791)
records.description: Deed executed 1 August 1791 (filed in Northumberland County that September) under Virginia's 1782 manumission act, freeing more than 500 people held by Robert Carter III on a gradual schedule by age — probably the largest private emancipation in the U.S. before the Civil War. Executors were still carrying it out decades later.

sources.label: Historic Christ Church — Robert Carter III's 1791 Deed of Gift

events.title: William Byrd I buys Westover
events.text: The Indian trader and importer of enslaved people buys the Westover tract on the James, seat of the Byrds until 1814.

events.title: Death of Robert 'King' Carter
events.text: Carter dies at Corotoman holding at least 295,000 acres and many hundreds of enslaved people, divided among children married into the Burwells, Pages, Harrisons and others.

events.title: Byrd advertises the new town of Richmond
events.text: William Byrd II offers lots in Richmond, laid out on his land at the falls of the James — later the Upper South's biggest slave market.

events.title: Patrick Henry: 'I cannot justify it'
events.text: Henry writes that he is 'master of slaves of my own purchase' and cannot justify it, yet holds 67 people at Red Hill at his death in 1799.

events.title: Mason condemns the slave trade at the Convention
events.text: On 22 August George Mason attacks the foreign slave trade; he later refuses to sign the Constitution — while enslaving dozens at Gunston Hall.

events.title: Robert Carter III's Deed of Gift
events.text: Carter begins the gradual freeing of more than 500 people — the largest private emancipation before the Civil War.

events.title: Revolt at Chatham
events.text: Enslaved people at William Fitzhugh's Chatham seize and whip an overseer who cut their Christmas holiday short; Abraham is executed and two men sold away.

events.title: Poisoning of George Wythe and Michael Brown
events.text: Wythe and the free youth Michael Brown die after arsenic poisoning; Black testimony is barred and the accused great-nephew is acquitted of murder.

source.label: Encyclopedia Virginia — The Death of George Wythe (1806)

events.title: Monroe sells 17 people to Florida
events.text: Indebted ex-president James Monroe sells 17 members of Highland's enslaved community to the Casa Bianca plantation in Jefferson County, Florida.

events.title: Skipwith family sent to Liberia
events.text: John Hartwell Cocke frees stonemason Peyton Skipwith and his family on condition they emigrate to Liberia; their letters home survive at UVA.

events.title: Lumpkin buys the Wall Street jail; Montpelier sold
events.text: Robert Lumpkin buys his Shockoe jail complex; the same year Dolley Madison sells Montpelier and breaks up its enslaved community.

events.title: Randolph Freedpeople driven from Mercer County
events.text: About 383 people freed by John Randolph of Roanoke's will reach Ohio but are turned away by armed whites and resettle near Piqua.

events.title: Hector Davis sells $2.67 million in people
events.text: One Richmond auction house's yearly sales of enslaved people exceed $2.67 million; Davis founds the Traders Bank in 1860.

events.title: A slave jail becomes a school
events.text: Mary Lumpkin leases Lumpkin's Jail to Nathaniel Colver for a school for freedmen — the origin of Virginia Union University.

events.title: Montpelier board shared with descendants
events.text: After a public dispute, the Montpelier Foundation elects 11 board members nominated by descendants of the people Madison enslaved.
